clips.display_text: Welcome to VSEPR theory. In this lab, we'll explore how electron pairs around a central atom arrange themselves in three-dimensional space. The central idea is simple: electron domains repel one another and settle into whatever geometry keeps them as far apart as possible.
clips.spoken_text: Welcome to vesper theory. In this lab, we'll explore how electron pairs around a central atom arrange themselves in three-dimensional space. The central idea is simple: electron domains repel one another and settle into whatever geometry keeps them as far apart as possible.

clips.display_text: Here's a flat Lewis structure of water. To count electron domains around the central oxygen atom, count each single bond, double bond, triple bond, or lone pair as one domain. Water has two bonding pairs and two lone pairs, for a total steric number of four.
clips.spoken_text: Here's a flat Lewis structure of water. To count electron domains around the central oxygen atom, count each single bond, double bond, triple bond, or lone pair as one domain. Water has two bonding pairs and two lone pairs, for a total steric number of four.

clips.display_text: VSEPR takes this flat, two-dimensional Lewis structure as input and predicts the real three-dimensional shape the molecule adopts. That's what we'll build up next.

clips.display_text: Let's watch two electron domains find their minimum-repulsion arrangement. They start at arbitrary positions near the central atom.
clips.spoken_text: Let's watch two electron domains find their minimum-repulsion arrangement. They start at arbitrary positions near the central atom.

clips.display_text: Repelled by one another, the two domains drift apart until they settle exactly opposite each other, 180 degrees apart. This is the linear electron-domain geometry.
clips.spoken_text: Repelled by one another, the two domains drift apart until they settle exactly opposite each other, one hundred eighty degrees apart. This is the linear electron-domain geometry.

clips.display_text: Now let's add a third domain. Watch as all three repel and rearrange into a trigonal planar shape, each 120 degrees from its neighbors.
clips.spoken_text: Now let's add a third domain. Watch as all three repel and rearrange into a trigonal planar shape, each one hundred twenty degrees from its neighbors.

clips.display_text: A fourth domain pushes the arrangement into three dimensions, producing a tetrahedron with bond angles of 109.5 degrees. This is the tetrahedral electron-domain geometry, the most common of all.
clips.spoken_text: A fourth domain pushes the arrangement into three dimensions, producing a tetrahedron with bond angles of one hundred nine point five degrees. This is the tetrahedral electron-domain geometry, the most common of all.

clips.display_text: Starting from our tetrahedron, let's add a fifth domain. Three domains move into an equatorial plane at 120 degrees to each other, while two more take axial positions at 90 degrees to that plane.
clips.spoken_text: Starting from our tetrahedron, let's add a fifth domain. Three domains move into an equatorial plane at one hundred twenty degrees to each other, while two more take axial positions at ninety degrees to that plane.

clips.display_text: Adding a sixth domain produces the octahedral geometry, where every neighboring domain is 90 degrees away. Feel free to rotate the molecule and inspect it from any angle.
clips.spoken_text: Adding a sixth domain produces the octahedral geometry, where every neighboring domain is ninety degrees away. Feel free to rotate the molecule and inspect it from any angle.

clips.display_text: Here is the complete catalog of electron-domain geometries: two domains give linear at 180 degrees, three give trigonal planar at 120, four give tetrahedral at 109.5, five give trigonal bipyramidal with both 90 and 120 degree angles, and six give octahedral at a uniform 90 degrees.
clips.spoken_text: Here is the complete catalog of electron-domain geometries: two domains give linear at one hundred eighty degrees, three give trigonal planar at one hundred twenty, four give tetrahedral at one hundred nine point five, five give trigonal bipyramidal with both ninety and one hundred twenty degree angles, and six give octahedral at a uniform ninety degrees.

clips.display_text: Here is methane, CH4. All four domains around carbon are bonding pairs to hydrogen atoms. The electron-domain geometry is tetrahedral, and since every domain is a bond, the molecular geometry is also tetrahedral. They match.
clips.spoken_text: Here is methane, C H four. All four domains around carbon are bonding pairs to hydrogen atoms. The electron-domain geometry is tetrahedral, and since every domain is a bond, the molecular geometry is also tetrahedral. They match.

clips.display_text: Now watch what happens when we replace one hydrogen with a lone pair, giving us ammonia, NH3. The electron-domain geometry is still tetrahedral, but the molecular geometry -- the shape traced by the atoms alone -- is now trigonal pyramidal.
clips.spoken_text: Now watch what happens when we replace one hydrogen with a lone pair, giving us ammonia, N H three. The electron-domain geometry is still tetrahedral, but the molecular geometry -- the shape traced by the atoms alone -- is now trigonal pyramidal.

clips.display_text: Replacing a second hydrogen with another lone pair gives us water, H2O. The electron-domain geometry remains tetrahedral throughout, but the molecular geometry is now bent. The lone pairs aren't seen as part of the molecular shape, but they still occupy space and influence it.

clips.display_text: Why does this happen? A lone pair is held only by the central atom's nucleus, unlike a bonding pair which is shared and pulled between two nuclei. With less nuclear pull constraining it, the lone pair spreads out more, occupying greater angular space and compressing the neighboring bond angles.

clips.display_text: Let's recap what we've covered. First, the minimum-repulsion principle: electron domains around a central atom arrange themselves to be as far apart as possible.

clips.display_text: Second, the five electron-domain geometries -- linear, trigonal planar, tetrahedral, trigonal bipyramidal, and octahedral -- each defined by domain count and characteristic angle.

clips.display_text: Third, the distinction between electron-domain geometry and molecular geometry -- they match only when every domain is a bonding pair. Fourth, lone pairs occupy more angular space than bonding pairs, compressing bond angles below idealized values.
